title: Cumulative frequency diagrams
summary: A [[cumulative-frequency|cumulative frequency]] is a running total of the frequencies. Its graph is a [[cumulative-frequency-diagram|cumulative frequency diagram]], and from the curve you estimate the [[median|median]], the [[quartile|quartiles]], the [[interquartile-range|interquartile range]] and any [[percentile|percentile]].

goals.text: Build a cumulative frequency table and use it to count values.
Use the curve to estimate how many values are below or above a given value.
Estimate the median, quartiles and interquartile range, and say what they show.
Estimate a percentile, and the percentage of values below a given value.

synonyms: how to draw a cumulative frequency graph
median from a cumulative frequency graph

before.hint: Put the values in order first.
before.explain: In order: $8, 11, 13, 17, 19, 22, 26$. The 4th of the $7$ values is $17$. Revise it in {{lesson:9.3}}.

before.prompt: The lower quartile of some data is $37$ and the upper quartile is $58$. Write down the interquartile range.
before.hint: Subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile.
before.explain: IQR $=$ upper quartile $-$ lower quartile $= 58 - 37 = 21$. Revise it in {{lesson:9.3}}.

blocks.text: A [[grouped-frequency-table|grouped frequency table]] counts the values in each class. Often you want something else: how many values are up to a certain size.

blocks.statement: The [[cumulative-frequency|cumulative frequency]] at a value is the number of data values less than or equal to it. It is a running total of the frequencies.
blocks.plain: Keep adding the frequencies as you move along the table.

blocks.text: Each running total belongs to the top of its class, the upper boundary. For $26 < t \le 30$, it counts every value up to $30$.

blocks.question: The finishing times of $68$ runners in a fun run are grouped below. $\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{Time } t\text{ (min)} & 22 < t \le 26 & 26 < t \le 30 & 30 < t \le 34 & 34 < t \le 38 & 38 < t \le 46 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 5 & 17 & 26 & 15 & 5 \end{array}$ Work out the cumulative frequency for each class.
steps: First class: $5$ runners took $26$ minutes or less.
Add the next frequency: $5 + 17 = 22$ took $30$ minutes or less.
Check: the last total equals the number of runners, $68$.

blocks.text: To count the values above a boundary, subtract its running total from the total frequency.

blocks.question: A courier weighs $93$ parcels. $\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{Mass } m\text{ (kg)} & m \le 1 & m \le 2 & m \le 4 & m \le 6 & m \le 9 \\ \hline \text{Cumulative frequency} & 11 & 34 & 67 & 85 & 93 \end{array}$ How many parcels have a mass of more than $4$ kg?
steps: $67$ parcels are $4$ kg or less.
Subtract from the total: $93 - 67 = 26$.

blocks.prompt: Use the courier's table. How many parcels are more than $2$ kg but at most $4$ kg?
blocks.hint: Both running totals count from the lightest parcel.
blocks.explain: $67$ are at most $4$ kg and $34$ are at most $2$ kg, so $67 - 34 = 33$.

blocks.text: A [[cumulative-frequency-diagram|cumulative frequency diagram]] draws the running totals as a curve.
1. Plot each cumulative frequency at the upper boundary of its class.
2. Plot the start too: the lowest boundary, with cumulative frequency $0$. No runner finished in $22$ minutes or less, so the race curve starts at $(22, 0)$, not $(0, 0)$.
3. Mark each point with a small cross. Join them with one smooth curve that never goes down.
Why the upper boundary? The total $22$ means $22$ runners had finished by $30$ minutes, the end of the class. It is not true at the middle, $28$.

blocks.question: Use the race-time table. Write down the point you plot for the class $34 < t \le 38$.
steps: The upper boundary of $34 < t \le 38$ is $38$. The running total there is $5 + 17 + 26 + 15 = 63$.

blocks.alt: Cumulative frequency diagram for the finishing times of 68 runners. Time in minutes across from 22 to 46, each small square 1 minute. Cumulative frequency up from 0 to 70, each small square 2 runners. Crosses at 22 minutes and 0, 26 and 5, 30 and 22, 34 and 48, 38 and 63, and 46 and 68, joined by a smooth S-shaped curve. The curve is steepest between 30 and 34 minutes. At 28 minutes it is at a height of about 12, and at 31 minutes about 28.
blocks.caption: It is steepest where the most runners finished.

blocks.text: To count from the curve, go up from a value to the curve, then across. The reading counts the values at or below it.

blocks.question: Use the race curve to estimate how many runners took more than $31$ minutes.
steps: Go up from $31$ minutes to the curve, then across. It reads about $28$.
So about $28$ runners took $31$ minutes or less.
The rest took longer: $68 - 28 = 40$.

blocks.text: Giving the reading, $28$, as the answer. It counts runners at or below $31$ minutes, so subtract it from the total.

blocks.prompt: Where do you plot the cumulative frequency for the class $38 < t \le 46$?
blocks.hint: Which time have all these runners finished by?
blocks.explain: Plot at the upper boundary, $46$, and the running total, $68$. $42$ is the midpoint, $38$ the lower boundary and $5$ the class frequency.

blocks.prompt: Use the race curve to estimate how many runners took more than $28$ minutes.
blocks.hint: Read up from $28$ and across, then subtract from $68$.
blocks.explain: About $12$ runners took $28$ minutes or less, so $68 - 12 = 56$ took longer.

blocks.text: For $n$ values, the [[median|median]] is the middle one. On the curve, go across from $\frac{1}{2}n$, halfway up the total.
The [[quartile|quartiles]] cut the data into quarters. Go across from $\frac{1}{4}n$ for the lower quartile (LQ) and $\frac{3}{4}n$ for the upper quartile (UQ).
For a list you used $\frac{n+1}{2}$. A curve gives only an estimate, so $\frac{1}{2}n$ is fine.
The [[interquartile-range|interquartile range]] is UQ $-$ LQ, read on the horizontal axis. It is the spread of the middle half of the data.

blocks.alt: Cumulative frequency diagram for the masses of 160 apples. Mass in grams across from 100 to 220, each small square 4 grams. Cumulative frequency up from 0 to 160, each small square 4 apples. Crosses at 100 grams and 0, 120 and 8, 140 and 38, 160 and 90, 180 and 136, 200 and 154, and 220 and 160, joined by a smooth S-shaped curve. Three dashed lines go across to the curve and down to the mass axis: from 40 down to about 141 grams, labelled LQ; from 80 down to about 156 grams, labelled median; from 120 down to about 172 grams, labelled UQ. The curve also passes about 20 at 130 grams, and reaches 144 at about 187 grams.
blocks.caption: Each dashed line starts at a running total and ends at an estimate.

blocks.question: A farm weighs $160$ apples. The diagram shows the results. Use it to estimate the median mass.
steps: Half of the total: $\frac{1}{2} \times 160 = 80$.
Draw a line from $80$ across to the curve, then down. With $4$ g per small square, it lands at about $156$ g.

blocks.question: Use the same diagram to estimate the interquartile range of the masses.
steps: Lower quartile: $\frac{1}{4} \times 160 = 40$. Across from $40$ and down gives about $141$ g.
Upper quartile: $\frac{3}{4} \times 160 = 120$. Across from $120$ and down gives about $172$ g.
The middle half of the apples cover about $31$ g.

blocks.text: Going across from $25$ and $75$ for the quartiles. Those are percentages, not counts. For $160$ apples, go across from $40$ and $120$.
To compare two data sets, use an average and a spread. A higher median means larger values on average. A smaller IQR means more consistent values.

blocks.prompt: A curve shows $240$ values. Which cumulative frequency gives the upper quartile?
blocks.hint: The upper quartile has three quarters of the values at or below it.
blocks.explain: $\frac{3}{4} \times 240 = 180$. $120$ and $60$ give the median and lower quartile, and $75$ is a percentage, not a count.

blocks.prompt: Farm B's apples have median $163$ g and IQR $22$ g. Farm A's have median $156$ g and IQR $31$ g. Which is correct?
blocks.hint: The median compares size. The IQR compares consistency.

options.text: B's are heavier on average and more consistent
B's are heavier on average but less consistent
A's are heavier on average and more consistent

blocks.explain: B's median is higher, so its apples are heavier on average. B's IQR is smaller, so their masses vary less.

verify.truth: B's are heavier on average and more consistent

blocks.text: Percentiles cut the data into hundredths, so you can ask about any percentage.

blocks.statement: The $p$th [[percentile|percentile]] is the value with $p\%$ of the data at or below it. Go across from $\frac{p}{100} \times n$.
blocks.plain: 90% of the data are at or below the 90th percentile.

blocks.text: The median is the $50$th percentile. The lower and upper quartiles are the $25$th and $75$th percentiles.

blocks.question: Use the apple diagram to estimate the $90$th percentile of the masses.
steps: Go across from $144$ to the curve, then down: about $187$ g.
So about $90\%$ of the apples weigh $187$ g or less.

blocks.text: You can also go the other way: read the count at a value, then write it as a percentage of the total.

blocks.question: Apples of $130$ g or less are sold for juice. Use the diagram to estimate the percentage of the $160$ apples sold for juice.
steps: Go up from $130$ g to the curve, then across: about $20$ apples.
As a percentage: $\frac{20}{160} \times 100 = 12.5\%$.

blocks.prompt: A curve shows $350$ scores. Which cumulative frequency gives the $60$th percentile?
Maya's reaction time is the $20$th percentile for her year. What does this mean?
blocks.hint: A percentile is a value with a percentage of the data at or below it.

options.text: About 20% of her year had a time at or below hers
Her time was 20% of the slowest time

blocks.explain: The $20$th percentile has $20\%$ of the data at or below it. It is not a position or a fraction of another time.

verify.truth: About 20% of her year had a time at or below hers

blocks.text: Cumulative frequency is a running total. The last one is the total frequency.
Plot at (upper boundary, cumulative frequency). Start at (lowest boundary, $0$) and join with a smooth curve.
IQR $=$ UQ $-$ LQ, both read on the horizontal axis. The $p$th percentile: go across from $\frac{p}{100} \times n$.
The curve counts values at or below a value. Number above it $=$ total $-$ reading.

mistakes: Plotting at the midpoint or lower boundary of a class. Plot at the upper boundary.
Starting at $(0, 0)$ when the first class starts higher. Start at the lowest boundary, with cumulative frequency $0$.
Going across from $25$, $50$ and $75$ whatever the total. Use $\frac{1}{4}$, $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{3}{4}$ of the total frequency.
Answering "how many are more than" with the reading. Subtract the reading from the total.
Giving the IQR as two values. It is one value: UQ minus LQ, read on the horizontal axis.
examTips: For **draw a cumulative frequency diagram**, the marks are for accurate points, including the start, and one smooth curve through them.
For **use your graph to find an estimate**, draw your reading lines on the graph. A reading close to the true one earns the mark, so read carefully against the small squares.
For **how many are more than** a value, show the reading and the subtraction from the total.
